changes.after: A name belongs to a part of the program called its scope. A new name inside braces can hide an outer name.

before: A variable declared inside braces is available within that block, not automatically outside it.
A new int score in an inner block is a different object. Updating it does not change the outer score.
An ordinary automatic local variable without an initializer does not provide a reliable initial value. Initialize it before use.
Keeping distinct names can make accidental shadowing easier to avoid. The example intentionally shows the difference between two objects.

Expected output or behavior: 7
3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare declaration and assignment in nested braces. Identify which object each printed name refers to. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Scope is the part of the code where a name is available. A variable declared inside a block of braces is available from that declaration to the end of the block.
Writing `int score = 7;` inside the inner block creates a second score. It hides the outer score while you are inside that block. This is called shadowing.
Initialize a variable by giving it a starting value. An ordinary local variable without one does not automatically start at zero. Give it a value before reading it.
This example uses the same name twice to show shadowing. In everyday code, different names can make it easier to see which value you are using.
The inner print reads the inner score, so it prints 7. After the inner block ends, the outer score is visible again and prints 3.
Remove int from the inner declaration. Then `score = 7;` updates the existing outer score instead of creating a second variable.
